title: Hybrid deployment evidence retention and access reconstruction standard
author: Maya Singh
body:
Summary
This document defines the standard evidence retention, packaging, and access-reconstruction procedures for incidents that span hybrid deployments (hosted, dedicated, and private/VPC). It reconciles RBAC snapshots, audit logging, and data residency constraints with forensic requirements and compliance evidence workflows.

Scope
- Applies to all incident classifications that require forensic reconstruction or regulatory evidence where services or data cross deployment boundaries.
- Covers audit logs, entitlement snapshots, endpoint-level telemetry, model artifacts, persistent storage, configuration state, and chain-of-custody artifacts.
- Excludes ephemeral in-memory traces unless explicitly requested by the incident commander and approved by Legal.

Definitions
- Hybrid deployment: any customer or internal workload that is served across more than one deployment mode (hosted + dedicated, hosted + private, or dedicated + private).
- Evidence bundle: a timeboxed collection of logs, snapshots, and metadata prepared for audit or legal review.
- Access reconstruction: the steps required to map a user/service action to artifacts (logs, entitlements, and network flows) to prove who/what performed an action.

Roles and ownership
- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates evidence collection, approves legal holds, ensures chain-of-custody continuity.
- Forensics Lead (Security): owns evidence bundle composition and integrity checks.
- Platform Owner (Infra/Eng): provides access to snapshots, storage, and retention policy enforcement.
- Customer Success / Account Security: flags customer-sensitive residency constraints.
- Legal / Compliance: approves retention beyond baseline and adjudicates cross-border transfer requests.

Retention matrix (baseline)
- Audit logs (ingestion-level): 365 days (hosted), 180 days (dedicated customer-managed), 90 days (edge/private default).
- RBAC snapshots (full entitlement graphs): 3 years for compliance-impacting incidents; otherwise 365 days.
- KV/cache access index (prefix/kv keys for reconstructions): 90 days.
- Model artifacts & provenance (manifest, hash, quantization profile): 5 years for production models used in regulated customers.
- Forensic disk images / VM snapshots: retained until case closure + 180 days (minimum 1 year if litigation expected).
- Legal hold: override baseline—retained until release by Legal.

Note: Retention windows are the minimum default. For hybrid deployments, retention is the intersection of the most restrictive jurisdictional residency and the technical mode (hosted vs customer-managed). Platform Owner must classify storage locations and mark evidence bundles with residency tags (e.g., eu, us, apac).

Evidence collection checklist (ordered)
1) Immediately create an incident evidence folder in the secure evidence store with a UUID and IC-assigned case ID.
2) Snapshot RBAC state at T0+0–5 minutes: identity provider claims, role bindings, service tokens, and temporary entitlements. Generate a signed digest (SHA256) and attach IC metadata.
3) Export ingestion and API gateway logs across all affected regions for T0-72h to T0+24h (default window).
4) Pull per-node/local runtime logs (stderr/stdout), model runtime traces, and cache eviction traces for affected nodes.
5) If private/dedicated, request customer-managed logs and attestations per the customer onboarding contract.
6) Preserve any ephemeral evidence (in-memory dump) only after Legal approval and using an approved preservation host.
7) Record transfer proof (S3 object hashes, transfer timestamps, TLS fingerprint) for every artifact moved across residency boundaries.

Chain-of-custody procedure
- Every evidence artifact MUST be recorded in the evidence ledger with: artifact ID, origin host/service, hash (SHA256), timestamp, collector identity, and transfer events.
- All collectors must sign the artifact metadata via platform signing key (automated where possible).
- When transferring across teams or exporting for legal/audit review, the Forensics Lead must generate a signed transfer manifest and obtain recipient acknowledgement.

Access reconstruction steps (technical runbook)
1) Correlate RBAC snapshot with authentication logs: map JWT/SAML/OIDC assertions to token exchange events.
2) Trace request path using API gateway trace IDs and service-level trace IDs; expand to host-level logs.
3) If KV/cache hits are relevant, consult prefix/KV access index to determine cache-primed prefixes and associated session IDs.
4) Reconstruct session timelines: sequence events, annotate with TTLs and observed latencies.
5) If model responses are in scope, include prompt inputs, model versioned manifest, and any reranking/reroute decisions.
6) Produce a narrative reconstruction document with supporting artifacts and a minimal reproducible timeline.

Technical configuration requirements (table)
- Audit log schema version: v3.2 (fields required: timestamp, trace_id, request_id, user_id, service, resource, action, result_code, client_ip, region, residency_tag).
- RBAC snapshot format: JSONL compressed + signed manifest.
- Evidence bundle packaging: tar.gz with manifest.json (signed), checksums, and chain-of-custody.csv.
- Storage encryption: AES-256 at rest, TLS1.3 in transit.
- Signature algorithm: rsa-4096 or ed25519 (preferred).

Exception and escalation (risk & exceptions)
- If retention or transfer conflicts with customer residency, initiate "Residency Exception" flow: submit an exception request including legal rationale, minimal artifact set, and proposed mitigations.
- Exception owners: Security + Legal + Product. Decisions must be recorded in the exception register and linked to the evidence bundle.
- Timebox for exception approval: 48 business hours for operational incidents; 7 business days for policy-level exceptions.

Automation & integrations
- SIEM ingestion: evidence bundles publish metadata to the SIEM; raw artifacts remain in secure evidence store with access gating.
- Orchestration: a set of Lambda/Cloud Functions to auto-snapshot RBAC, collect API gateway slices, and compute checksums. These tasks must be idempotent and reversible.
- Retention enforcement: lifecycle policies on evidence buckets enforce delete dates unless Legal hold flag exists. Audit retention TTL must be immutable for the period recorded in the manifest.

Verification and auditability
- Monthly integrity sweep: Forensics engineers run a checksum verification across a randomized 10% of evidence bundles older than 90 days. Failures trigger an incident for corruption investigation.
- Quarterly policy review: Security and Legal review retention matrix and residency tags.

Templates and artifacts (links)
- Evidence bundle manifest template (JSON) — /confluence/templates/evidence-manifest.json
- RBAC snapshot collector script — /confluence/eng-infra/automation/rbac-snapshot-collector.sh
- Chain-of-custody CSV template — /confluence/templates/chain-of-custody.csv

FAQ
- Q: Can customer-managed dedicated logs be forcibly ingested into hosted evidence store?
  A: No. We require customer approval or contractual entitlement. If unavailable, collect attestations and metadata from the customer and include in the bundle.
- Q: Who can release a Legal hold?
  A: Only Legal can release a hold; Forensics Lead may request release after closing activities.

Revision history
- 2026-03-15: Created by Maya Singh.
- 2026-07-01: Added automated RBAC snapshot guidance and SIEM integration notes.
- 2026-10-02: Aligned retention matrix with new data-sovereignty baseline and added verification sweep.

Appendix: quick checklists
- Incident start (first 30 minutes): create evidence folder, RBAC snapshot, ingest gateway logs, tag residency.
- 24-hour checklist: collect node-level logs, model manifests, customer attestations, and compute bundle checksums.
- Closure checklist: Legal hold review, manifest signoff, retention policy assignment, archive scheduling.
